post.title: nl2shell: Plain English In, Safe Shell Commands Out
post.description: How I built nl2shell.com: a fine-tuned 0.8B model that turns plain English into shell commands, with a regex danger check and a network-less Docker sandbox.
post.excerpt: Developers alt-tab to ChatGPT for tar flags and find predicates, and that is overkill for a narrow task. nl2shell serves a fine-tuned 0.8B model for free, warns you before you copy anything dangerous, and executes in a network-less Docker sandbox. Here is how it works, and what a small model taught me about safety.
post.content:
I keep a mental list of commands I refuse to memorize. The exact tar flags. Most find predicates. Every awk incantation ever written. The usual fix is to alt-tab out of the terminal and ask ChatGPT. That works, but it is overkill: a frontier model behind an API key or a subscription, extra latency, and your intent shipped to a third party, all for a one-liner.

nl2shell is my bet that a narrow task, natural language to shell, does not need a frontier model. Type plain English at [nl2shell.com](https://nl2shell.com), get the command back from a fine-tuned 0.8B-parameter model served free, with a danger check before you copy and a network-less Docker sandbox if you want to run it.

## Try it first

```bash
curl -X POST https://nl2shell-web.vercel.app/api/translate \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "find all python files"}'
```

I ran that on 2026-07-11. It returned:

```json
{"command":"find . -name \"*.py\"","meta":"Device: CPU | 8 tokens | 1.2 tok/s | 6.52s"}
```

The same endpoint on nl2shell.com gave me `find . -type f -exec du -h {} \;` for "list files by size" in 2.70 seconds. Notice the meta field: the API prints its own latency and token rate right in the payload. The free tier is slow, and the response says so.

## The bet: small model, narrow task

The model is a Qwen3.5-0.8B fine-tune trained with QLoRA (per the README). At that size it is cheap enough to serve free on Hugging Face's CPU tier and small enough to run locally through Ollama as a GGUF. No API keys, no subscription.

The catch: the output of this tool is executable and potentially destructive. So safety is not a footnote here. It is half the product.

## How it works

1. **Translate.** The web app is Next.js 16 on Vercel. `POST /api/translate` validates the query (500 characters max), rate-limits at 30 requests per minute per IP, then calls a Gradio Space (AryaYT/nl2shell-demo) on Hugging Face's free CPU tier via `@gradio/client`. The rate limiter keys on Vercel's `x-real-ip`; a code comment explicitly refuses `x-forwarded-for` because it is client-spoofable.

2. **Clean.** Raw output from a 0.8B model is messy. `cleanResponse()` in `lib/clean-response.ts` strips Qwen `<think>` blocks (including unclosed ones when the model truncates mid-thought), markdown code fences, wrapping backticks, leading `$` and `>` prompt characters, "Here is the command:" preambles, and stray leading comment lines. It is 41 unglamorous lines, a museum of small-model failure modes, and it is what makes a 0.8B model usable.

3. **Warn.** Before anything is displayed, `lib/safety.ts` checks the command against 21 regex patterns: recursive or forced `rm`, `sudo`, `dd if=`, `mkfs`, fork bombs, `chmod 777`, writes to raw disk devices, `curl | sh`, reboot and shutdown, `fdisk`. `getDangerReason()` maps each match to a human-readable warning like "Piped remote code execution", so you know why you are being warned before you copy.

4. **Execute, if you choose.** Execution goes through a separate Hono relay server. Each session gets its own Docker container created with `--network none`, `--cap-drop ALL`, `--security-opt no-new-privileges`, 512MB of memory, 1 CPU, a 100-process pid limit, and output piped through `head -n 200`. The `/api/execute` route is rate-limited to 10 per minute with a 4096-character command cap.

## Two safety lists, two threat models

This is the design decision I would defend hardest: two independent regex layers that do not protect the same thing.

The display-time list protects the human: `sudo`, `rm -rf`, reboot, and piped remote code get a visible warning before you copy. The execution-time list (16 patterns in `relay/security.ts`) protects the sandbox: it hard-blocks `docker`, `kubectl`, `nsenter`, `mount`, and `chown root`, the escape vectors the display list does not care about. A human copying `docker ps` into their own terminal is fine. A sandboxed process invoking Docker is not.

## Run it locally

The web app:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nl2shell/nl2shell-web.git
cd nl2shell-web && bun install && bun dev
```

It runs with zero environment variables. HF_TOKEN and Supabase are optional.

The model, via Ollama:

```bash
ollama run hf.co/AryaYT/nl2shell-0.8b
```

The Q4_K_M GGUF is roughly half a gigabyte. There is also an install script at `public/install.sh` that sets up Ollama and pulls the model. My favorite detail in either repo: it downloads Ollama's installer to a `mktemp` file and runs it locally, deliberately avoiding the `curl | sh` pattern that nl2shell's own safety list flags as "Piped remote code execution". (I have not executed the script end-to-end, so treat it as documented rather than verified.)

There is also `lib/os-context.ts`, which fingerprints the host: distro, package manager, shell, whether you have sudo or Docker. That context conditions the prompt, so "install htop" can resolve to `brew` on macOS and `apt` on Debian.

## The pipeline behind the model

The second repo, nl2shell-terminal-lab, is where the model comes from.

`tb-dataset/generate.py` synthesizes multi-step terminal-task trajectories using pydantic-schema-constrained Gemini on Vertex AI, weighted to match the category and difficulty distribution of the 241 real Terminal-Bench tasks without copying any of them.

Then decontamination, a first-class feature here, not a checkbox:

```bash
python tb-dataset/merge_dedup.py
```

It rejects any row containing the Terminal-Bench canary string or sharing any 8-gram with a real benchmark instruction, then semantic-dedups (token-set ratio above 0.9) and writes a 90/10 split. The committed corpus is 8,127 SFT rows (7,335 train, 792 val, verified with `wc -l`). The docs lag: the README still says 652 rows, because the pipeline outran its own documentation overnight.

Overnight is literal. Training ran as Vertex AI managed distillation, a thinking teacher generating reasoning traces for a small student. HANDOFF.md describes a self-rescheduling agent loop that kept about 16 concurrent tuning jobs alive to drain a $300 GCP free-trial credit before it expired, and REPORT.html logs the burn: $230 down to $151.81, 26 jobs, 272 GiB of checkpoints, with `ops/spend_monitor.py` enforcing a budget cap the whole time.

Evaluation is by execution, not text similarity:

```bash
python eval/tb_eval.py --base-url http://localhost:1234/v1 --model nl2shell --limit 50
```

It runs the model over Terminal-Bench-style tasks, executes each task's verification command in a disposable `docker run --rm` sandbox with a 60-second timeout, and scores real pass or fail. A `--gguf` flag supports local llama.cpp models.

## Agents as first-class users

The site assumes its users include other AIs. `app/api/mcp/route.ts` is a JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP server exposing `leshell_translate`, `leshell_execute`, and `leshell_explain`, discoverable through `public/agents.txt`, `public/llms.txt`, and `.well-known/ai-plugin.json`. (Yes, the internal codename is "leshell". The LeSearch naming shows through, and I have decided to find it charming.)

For humans there is voice input via the Web Speech API, copy-to-clipboard, and a session-only history of your last 20 commands. Thumbs up or down plus corrections persist to Supabase, and the README ships the SQL to harvest those corrections as future training data.

## Honest limitations

- The safety layer is regex blocklisting, not semantic analysis. It catches known-bad shapes but can be bypassed through obfuscation: base64, variable expansion, aliases.
- The free Hugging Face CPU tier is slow. My live tests measured 2.7 to 6.5 seconds per query at 1.2 to 5.2 tokens per second, the Space sleeps after 48 hours of inactivity with roughly a 30-second cold start, and the README openly says it queues under load.
- Rate limiting is an in-memory Map that resets on every serverless cold start. A code comment already recommends Upstash Redis for production.
- The in-browser WebGPU mode does not run the fine-tuned model. It currently loads a generic Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with a system prompt.
- No accuracy number or Terminal-Bench score for the fine-tuned model is published in either repo. The eval harness exists; a committed eval report does not.
- Sandboxed execution needs a separately hosted relay (`SANDBOX_RELAY_URL`, default localhost:4000). Only `/api/translate` was verified live for this post, and the relay deployment was still a planned step in NEXT-STEPS.md.

## What's next

Three obvious moves. Deploy the relay (NEXT-STEPS.md points at Railway) so sandboxed execution works in production and not just on localhost. Point the browser engine at the actual fine-tuned model instead of the generic fallback. And run the eval harness against nl2shell-0.8b and commit the report, because a project this opinionated about benchmark hygiene should publish its own score.

The bigger loop is already wired: every thumbs-down correction lands in Supabase, and the README already ships the SQL to turn those corrections into future training data. The tool is set up to teach the model that powers it.

Code: [aryateja2106/nl2shell-web](https://github.com/aryateja2106/nl2shell-web) and [aryateja2106/nl2shell-terminal-lab](https://github.com/aryateja2106/nl2shell-terminal-lab). Try it at [nl2shell.com](https://nl2shell.com).

Three things I learned building it:

1. Narrow task, small model. A Qwen3.5-0.8B QLoRA fine-tune handles NL-to-shell on Hugging Face's free CPU tier, or locally via Ollama (the GGUF is roughly half a gigabyte). No API keys, no subscription.

2. Safety needs two lists. One regex layer warns the human before they copy (rm -rf and curl piped to sh get named reasons like "Piped remote code execution"). A separate list protects the Docker sandbox from escape vectors: docker, nsenter, mount are hard-blocked. The sandbox itself runs with no network and all capabilities dropped.

3. Benchmark hygiene is a feature. Every synthetic training row is checked against the Terminal-Bench canary string and 8-gram overlap before it enters the 8,127-row corpus.
